extracted.intended_audience: economists, policymakers, entrepreneurs, and researchers interested in blockchain market design and crypto tokens
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for when and how blockchain (permissionless and permissioned) technologies add value to markets, including design trade-offs, security, privacy, governance, and bootstrapping considerations. Useful for assessing suitability of blockchain architecture and token-based incentives for a specific application or market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less concentrated market power in permissionless networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissionless implementations are “less likely to leave market power in the hands of their founders or early participants.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits any party's ability to unilaterally censor transactions or exclude participants and removes single points of failure. The text links concentrated intermediary power to higher prices, user lock-in, censorship risk, and reduced resilience. Evaluate whether a design materially reduces a single actor's control and associated market-power harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on on-chain rules versus off-chain governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissionless networks are “less reliant on off-chain governance, relational contracts and laws” because they embed incentives and governance rules into protocol code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While permissionless systems still need off-chain coordination for hard forks or controversial changes, designs that codify more rules reduce discretion of any single party. Assess how much decision-making is encoded on-chain, what requires off-chain coordination, and the feasibility of executing off-chain actions (e.g., hard forks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy model and deanonymization risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which shared ledger data is public and pseudonymous (as in Bitcoin) versus shielded for anonymity (as in Zcash) is a market design choice; many ledgers are pseudonymous and susceptible to deanonymization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the ledger's privacy guarantees meet application needs. Consider available privacy technologies (zk-STARKs, mixers, Zcash, Monero) and the residual deanonymization risk from public transaction histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural impact on firm value capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Blockchain implementations that reduce the cost of networking “induce architectural changes in how firms create and capture value,” opening opportunities for entrants and new business models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a blockchain architecture materially changes incumbents' assets and knowledge (architectural innovation), whether it separates benefits of network effects from costs of market power, and how it reshapes competition and rent allocation among users, developers, and investors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bootstrapping incentives via native tokens
rubrics_metrics.description: During bootstrapping, a native token “can be used to create incentives for adoption and to fund the development and scaling of the network,” e.g., mining rewards or ICOs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a project, examine the token’s role in funding and incentivizing early adopters and contributors (analogous to founder/employee equity). Check whether rewards are well-aligned with desired contributions and whether token distribution mechanisms are robust to gaming, imitation, and low-cost forks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early-adopter and investor motivations and risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Early adopters may contribute for consumption utility, signalling, or to create alternatives; investors may join for expected appreciation. Individuals can be both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the composition and incentives of early participants. Consider whether reliance on speculative appreciation (versus productive contributions) makes the project vulnerable to volatility, fraud, or a shift from R&D to short-term speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud, low entry barriers, and token valuation volatility
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of low entry barriers, ease of writing smart-contract ICOs, and uncertain regulation, bad actors and speculators have entered the space; token valuations have been extremely volatile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate project's vulnerability to fraudulent imitators and speculative bubbles. Examine regulatory exposure, transparency, team credibility, and mechanisms that distinguish high-quality projects from poor imitators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustaining incentives and avoiding tragedy of the commons
rubrics_metrics.description: In the operational phase, a key challenge is “ensuring that the incentives continue to support contributions of key resources to the ecosystem, and avoiding a tragedy of the commons.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess long-run incentive sustainability for public-good protocol improvements (security, throughput, latency). Consider governance, funding models, and whether contributors have ongoing incentives to invest in shared infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate conditions for blockchain adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Blockchain adds substantial value under fairly narrow conditions: (1) when last-mile problems are not severe and digital verification can be implemented in a novel or more fine-grained way; (2) when reduction in cost of networking allows more efficient allocation of rents between users, developers, and investors; (3) when the combination of reductions in verification and networking costs enables new digital assets/property rights; (4) when there is a need for greater privacy and user control over data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four conditions as a checklist to judge whether a proposed application is a good fit for blockchain. If none are met, centralized solutions are likely preferable due to decentralization costs and governance complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical performance requirements (throughput, latency, cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The technology will need to reach a level of performance (e.g. throughput, latency, cost per transaction, etc.) comparable to traditional networks.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the blockchain meets application-specific performance targets (transactions/sec, latency, per-transaction cost). Consider whether decentralization-induced inefficiencies are outweighed by benefits (privacy, competition, censorship resistance). Hybrid designs may be acceptable transitional solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory clarity and investor protection
rubrics_metrics.description: “Regulatory frameworks will have to evolve to reduce uncertainty for founders and network participants, and to provide stronger protections for investors and early adopters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess applicable securities/financial regulation risk, compliance strategy, and how token design maps to existing legal categories. Evaluate investor protections, disclosure, and mechanisms to deter fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security model: mining/computing power dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: In proof-of-work systems, the blockchain's security is “only as secure as the amount of computing power dedicated to mining it,” generating economies of scale and positive feedback between value and security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating security, quantify the cost to perform a successful attack (e.g., 51% attack), look at miner distribution, and consider feedback loops: higher token value attracts miners which increases security; loss of value can cascade to insecurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus parameter trade-offs (block interval and block size)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The interval at which a new block is added to the chain and the maximum number of transactions that can be included in a block endogenously determine the optimal transaction type on a specific blockchain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match block interval and block size choices to transaction types and security needs. The paper contrasts Bitcoin (10 min, 1MB) with Litecoin (2.5 min) to illustrate security vs bandwidth trade-offs, and notes Layer-2 solutions (e.g., Lightning) as scaling approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy design choice as a market design parameter
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of publicly visible data versus shielded anonymity on a ledger is a deliberate market design choice that affects who can read transaction histories and deanonymize participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether public, pseudonymous, or cryptographically private ledger suits the use case. Consider third-party risks for deanonymization and the availability/feasibility of privacy-preserving tech like zk-STARKs or mixers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance trade-offs: forking vs lock-in
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissionless networks allow participants to participate in governance (often proportional to stake) and minorities can fork the codebase; forks reduce lock-in but introduce uncertainty and may lower network value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess governance mechanisms, stake-based participation, the costs and consequences of potential forks, and whether off-chain coordination is sufficient to handle contentious changes without destroying confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usability and custody trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many blockchain implementations “lack the convenience and usability of the centralized solutions consumers are used to,” and users often rely on third-party wallets, reintroducing trust in intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating adoption prospects, consider user experience, key management complexity, need for custodial services, and whether usability barriers undermine privacy/self-custody benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role for intermediaries providing complementary services
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediaries can still add substantial value by focusing on tasks complementary to digital verification (e.g., secure recording of offline events, curation, certification of identity and services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which complementary services remain necessary and whether incumbents or new intermediaries can provide them competitively. Consider threat to intermediaries' revenue sources and their potential adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards perspective: one chain does not fit all transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: A single blockchain will not perfectly accommodate every type of transaction; transaction size, attributes, functionality, and required security/privacy push different marketplaces to different blockchains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether specialization (different chains or layer-2s) better fits application needs and factor cross-chain interoperability, security economies of scale, and fragmentation costs into design decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mining output usefulness and security trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: If mining outputs were useful for other purposes, marginal cost of mining would be lower, but the network could remain as secure because miners would dedicate more resources as returns increase; the sunk, wasteful cost of PoW is what defends the ledger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider arguments about proof-of-stake and alternative consensus: evaluate trade-offs between waste (PoW) and different security incentives (PoS), and how useful external outputs of mining would alter incentives and attack costs.
